sections.title: Landscape
sections.text: Photonic metamaterial surfaces have emerged as critical substrates for label-free imaging, primarily through two distinct modalities: photonic crystal-enhanced microscopy (PCEM) and dielectric metasurface-based refractometry. PCEM utilizes a photonic crystal biosensor surface as a substrate to enable quantitative, submicron-resolution, and time-resolved imaging of cell-surface interactions without the need for dyes or stains [4]. The system is typically integrated into standard microscope bodies, such as the Carl Zeiss Axio Observer Z1, to facilitate these measurements [3]. In parallel, dielectric metasurfaces offer a platform for label-free sensing through refractometric, surface-enhanced spectroscopy, and chiral schemes [2]. These metasurfaces rely on the physics of optical Mie scattering from subwavelength resonators, which exhibit strong responses to both electric and magnetic fields, a property that distinguishes them from plasmonic counterparts that respond weakly to magnetic fields [2]. The spectral position of defect modes in these structures is highly sensitive to local environmental changes, such as refractive index shifts caused by analyte binding, making them effective transduction signals [1].

snippets: Since spectral position of the defect mode is highly sensitive to the change in the local environment around the "defect", it can be used as the sensing transduction signal when the RI changes as a result of the binding of the molecules to the defect.

sections.title: Comparison
sections.text: PCEM offers unique advantages over other microscopy techniques by providing a direct quantification and two-dimensional localization of cell attachment at the single-cell level [4]. Unlike surface plasmon resonance imaging (SPRi), which requires illumination to pass through cell structures and suffers from limited lateral resolution due to plasmon propagation distances, PCEM avoids these artifacts [4]. Similarly, while atomic force microscopy (AFM) provides information about biological surfaces, it does not directly analyze the interaction between cells and their substrates and is limited in throughput by probe scanning [4]. PCEM is particularly effective for extended time-course studies where label-based assays are not feasible, such as observing cell migration over days [4]. In terms of refractometric sensing, dielectric metasurfaces allow for precise engineering of resonance wavelengths from the visible to the infrared spectrum by adjusting feature sizes [2]. The quality factor (Q factor) of these resonances directly influences the resolution for measuring refractive index changes [2]. Furthermore, high-index all-dielectric metasurfaces avoid the optical losses associated with free charges found in plasmonic systems [5].

In particular, when combined with a small-scale light source – i.e., laser or light-emitting diode (LED) – and an imaging camera (i.e., complementary metal-oxide-semiconductor (CMOS) or charge-coupled device (CCD) cameras), the intensity-based optical readers can be ultra-compact, low-weight, and portable by eliminating the need for sophisticated spectroscopy instrumentations
Thus, spectrometer-less readers can reduce cost and improve mechanical robustness

Compared to single-unit metasurfaces, such diatomic structures provide advanced flexibility in the engineering of the in-plane asymmetry while keeping the design easier to fabricate and make it more feasible for biosensing applications.

sections.title: Open Gaps
sections.text: Despite the advancements in photonic surfaces, certain technical limitations and challenges remain. For PCEM, the method relies on noncoherent illumination of the photonic crystal biosensor coupled with a spectroscopic scanning system to achieve its capabilities [4]. The sensitivity of the system is characterized by photonic wavelength shifts (PWV), with average shifts of approximately 0.12 nm over 12 hours and a standard deviation of 0.09 nm in uniform media [3] [4]. While PCEM can resolve boundaries of approximately 0.5 nm PWV shifts, other forms of microscopy do not provide direct measurements of live cell-surface attachment localization and strength with the same dynamic morphological detail [4]. In the context of metasurfaces, the development of ultrasensitive biosensors faces challenges that require specific solutions to optimize performance [6]. Additionally, while dielectric metasurfaces offer low loss, the integration of these surfaces into portable, spectrometer-less readers is an area of active development to reduce cost and improve mechanical robustness [5].

sections.title: Dynamics
sections.text: The dynamic capabilities of photonic metamaterial surfaces are highlighted by their ability to monitor biological processes in real-time. PCEM provides rich, dynamic information about the evolution of cell-surface attachment profiles over biologically relevant time scales [4]. As cells attach and spread, positive PWV shifts are observed due to the increased concentration of cellular material within the evanescent field region of the photonic crystal [4]. This method retains sufficient spatial resolution to observe attachment footprints of filopodial extensions and intracellular attachment strength gradients [4]. PCEM has been used to enable the first label-free time-lapse imaging of attachment localization in living cells during chemotaxis [3]. It allows for continuous monitoring of spatial gradients in cell-surface attachment and the extension of fine-structured filopodia over extended periods compatible with processes like apoptosis and differentiation [3]. Because the technology is label-free, populations of cells can be measured repeatedly without disrupting their culture environment [3]. In metasurface-based systems, intensity-based readers can detect analyte binding through spatially resolved intensity changes at a fixed wavelength, offering a compact and portable alternative to traditional spectroscopic methods [5].
